question:
Patient note:
A 79-year-old woman, widowed and living alone in a single-story apartment, was seen this afternoon in the combined vascular–pulmonary clinic at the request of her podiatrist after she reported needing more frequent rests when walking from her driveway to the mailbox. She attributes this progressive left-calf tightness to “poor circulation” first identified ten years ago when ankle–brachial indices measured 0.62 on the right and 0.54 on the left; three years later she underwent balloon angioplasty of the superficial femoral artery but refused stent placement because the procedure restored only limited symptom-free walking distance. Since that time she has limited herself to short neighborhood strolls with a rollator and applies 30-mm Hg knee-high compression stockings each morning; she has no history of gangrene or lower-extremity amputation, yet two small fissures at the base of the left fifth metatarsal required weekly debridement last winter. She smoked one pack per day from age 18 to 68—approximately 50 pack-years in total—quitting when forced to use a short prednisone taper after an emergency department visit for wheezing and prolonged cough; pulmonary function testing afterward showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.55 with an FEV1 of 49 % predicted that improved by only 3 % following bronchodilator, and she now inhales tiotropium 18 µg each morning, budesonide–formoterol 160/4.5 µg twice daily, and uses albuterol about four times per week when climbing the two small steps into her porch. She has never required home oxygen or non-invasive nocturnal ventilation, though she keeps a three-day “rescue pack” of doxycycline and prednisone supplied by her primary physician for winter exacerbations, of which she has needed two in the past five years without hospitalization. Type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 22 years ago during pre-operative blood work for cataract removal; her regimen progressed from diet to metformin, then to insulin glargine 24 units nightly combined with sitagliptin 100 mg each morning. A hemoglobin A1c measured last month was 8.4 %. She underwent pan-retinal photocoagulation six years ago for proliferative retinopathy, inserts custom molded shoe inserts for distal sensory neuropathy that causes numb toes, and urinates clear urine without foaming; a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio two weeks ago was 110 mg/g, while serum creatinine today is 1.0 mg/dL with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 68 mL/min/1.73 m². For the past decade comprehensive metabolic panels have shown borderline aminotransferase elevations—current AST 46 U/L, ALT 48 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and albumin 4.2 g/dL—attributed to biopsy-proven non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; she denies pruritus, easy bruising, abdominal distention, or encephalopathic episodes, and abdominal ultrasound last spring confirmed smooth hepatic contours without portal vein dilation or splenomegaly. She has never experienced crushing substernal discomfort, diaphoresis on exertion, or catheter-based coronary intervention, and an echocardiogram obtained for presurgical clearance two years ago demonstrated normal biventricular size and an ejection fraction of 58 % without segmental wall-motion abnormality. There is no history of sudden unilateral weakness, slurred speech, facial droop, seizures, or visual field loss, and cognitive screening with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment performed last year scored 27/30; she independently manages complex medication schedules, pays household bills online, and recalls recent news events in conversation. She abstains from alcohol, denies intravenous drug use, and her vaccination record is current through last season’s high-dose influenza formulation. Family history is notable for a brother who required aorto-bifemoral bypass at 71 and a father who died of emphysema in his early seventies; there is no familial clustering of hepatic cirrhosis, hematologic malignancy, or immunodeficiency. Current medications include aspirin 81 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily initiated after the prior angioplasty, rosuvastatin 20 mg nightly, insulin and sitagliptin as noted, tiotropium, budesonide–formoterol, albuterol, vitamin D 1000 IU daily, and over-the-counter fish oil; she is allergic to sulfonamide antibiotics, which caused widespread hives decades ago. On examination she sits upright, breathing comfortably in full sentences. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 138/74 mm Hg seated in the right arm, heart rate 82 beats/min and regular, respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 94 % on ambient air, body-mass index 25 kg/m². Carotid pulses are brisk without bruit; the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S1 and S2 are crisp, and no murmurs, gallops, or rubs are evident. Lungs reveal diminished breath sounds at the bases with scattered end-expiratory wheezes but no crackles. The abdomen is soft, non-tender, with a palpable liver edge 1 cm below the right costal margin that is smooth and non-nodular. Examination of the lower limbs shows cool, hairless shins, shiny thin skin, dependent rubor, and pallor on elevation; pedal pulses are absent, femoral pulses are diminished, capillary refill exceeds five seconds at the toes, and dependent duplex Doppler signals are monophasic. Two superficial calluses with serous crust over the left lateral foot measure 0.3 cm each without surrounding erythema. Neurologic testing identifies reduced vibration sense to the ankles, absent pinprick at the distal toes, preserved proprioception at the great toes, normal strength proximally and distally, and a steady tandem gait limited only by calf discomfort after ten meters. A point-of-care ankle–brachial index performed during the visit reads 0.48 on the left and 0.55 on the right. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 80 beats/min with preserved intervals and no Q waves or ST-T changes. She presents today seeking guidance on whether repeat endovascular intervention or supervised treadmill therapy might extend her pain-free walking time, and asks whether ongoing inhaler therapy is adequate to protect her lungs during an upcoming move closer to her daughter’s coastal home.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) adds age points to the weights for qualifying chronic diseases present at presentation.
- Age 79: the 70–79 age band adds 3 points.
- Peripheral vascular disease: claudication, bilateral ankle–brachial indices below 0.6, and prior femoral angioplasty establish symptomatic arterial disease = 1 point.
- Chronic pulmonary disease: persistent airflow obstruction with FEV1/FVC 0.55 and maintenance inhaler use supports COPD = 1 point.
- Diabetes with end-organ damage: proliferative retinopathy and distal sensory neuropathy qualify = 2 points. Uncomplicated diabetes is not counted separately.
- Mild liver disease: biopsy-proven fatty liver disease without portal hypertension or decompensation = 1 point.
- Other CCI conditions = 0 points. In particular, albuminuria with creatinine 1.0 mg/dL and eGFR 68 does not qualify for separate moderate-to-severe renal disease points.
Total = 3 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 8.
Final answer: 8
